title: The stones became one (Genesis Rabbah 68:11)
hook: stones quarrel over who will be Jacob's pillow, and become one stone
tomorrow: same night, a ladder. why is Jacob scared to climb it?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the palace has an owner, and the owner answers the one who asks. Today, that asker's grandson, sleeping out in the open.

Two siblings, one back seat, one armrest: a whole war over a few inches of plastic. Genesis has a stranger quarrel, hidden in the grammar. Jacob, running from his brother, stops for the night. In the King James wording, "he took of the stones of that place, and put them for his pillows." Stones, plural. Next morning he "took the stone that he had put for his pillows." One stone. Where did the rest go?
screen: `ONE ARMREST, TWO SIBLINGS.` → `STONES AT NIGHT.` → `ONE STONE IN THE MORNING?`

segments.voice: Genesis Rabbah has an answer, one of the midrashim you could tell a kid at bedtime. The stones started quarreling. Each one said: let this righteous man lay his head on me. On me, not you. And in the night, the Holy One made them one stone, so nobody lost. Notice what the stones are fighting about. Not about being left out, or stuck with the job. Each one wants to be the one that serves. It's a quarrel between good intentions, the kind families have all the time: two people who both want to host the holiday, two siblings who both want to drive Dad to the doctor. And the midrash doesn't pick a winner. No stone is told: you were right. They're joined, and the head rests on all of them at once. The grammar puzzle has a story behind it. The plural turns singular because something happened in the night, and the midrash fills that gap with peace. It sits right before the ladder, too. Before Jacob dreams of heaven, the ground under his head stops fighting.
screen: `STONES, THEN ONE STONE.` · `EACH ONE WANTS TO SERVE.` · `NO WINNER. JOINED.` · `PEACE BEFORE THE LADDER.` · then, large: `THE STONES BECAME ONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small quarrel you're in, where both of you want something good. Draft a text to that person, in your head or on your phone without sending: one line that names what you both want. Let it sit there for the rest of the sit; whether it goes is for later.
The stones became one: the midrash's answer to Genesis 28. Stones that fought over who would serve, joined in the night.
Keep this one: the stones became one, and nobody had to lose. See you tomorrow.

notes: Genesis Rabbah 68:11 paraphrased (the stones each say 'let this righteous one rest his head on me'; they are made one). The midrash also has other views (e.g. a set number of stones joining as a sign); left out. Confirm.

Genesis 28:11 and 28:18 quoted from the KJV because it keeps the Hebrew plural visible ('stones… pillows'); JPS 1917 renders 28:11 'one of the stones of the place'. Confirm this choice for the Jewish path.
